title: Non-chill filtered whisky and haze | Craft Beer School
desc: What chill filtration does, why some whiskies skip it and why a non-chill filtered whisky can turn cloudy with water or ice.
teaser: Your whisky went cloudy when you added ice. Nothing is wrong with it. Here is why.
standfirst: Many whiskies are chilled and filtered before bottling so they stay clear in the cold. Others skip that step and say so on the label. Here is what chill filtration removes, why it matters to some drinkers and what the haze in your glass actually is.
sections:
Chill filtration cools whisky, often to around 0 °C or below, then passes it through fine filters. At low temperature, some compounds come out of solution and form a faint haze. The filters catch them. The whisky that comes through stays clear even if it later gets cold on a shelf, in a shop window in winter or over ice.

It is a cosmetic step. Its job is to stop a customer returning a bottle because it looked cloudy. Our guide to chill filtration and caramel colouring covers both common bottling steps.

The haze is mostly long-chain fatty acid esters, along with some fatty acids and other compounds from the spirit and the wood. Esters such as ethyl dodecanoate and ethyl hexadecanoate dissolve well in strong spirit but less well as the alcohol drops or the temperature falls.

These compounds are not harmful. They are part of the spirit. Some drinkers and distillers believe they add body, mouthfeel and flavour, which is why removing them is debated.

Chill filtration also removes fine particles of char and wood that every cask sheds. Most whiskies, chill filtered or not, pass through a coarse filter for that reason. The difference lies in whether the whisky is chilled first, which is what pulls the esters out.

You will see many non-chill filtered whiskies bottled at 46% ABV or higher. The usual explanation is that at around 46% and above, those esters stay dissolved at normal room temperature, so the whisky stays clear without chill filtration. Below that strength, haze is more likely when the bottle gets cold.

That makes 46% a practical line rather than a legal one. Scotch can be bottled at any strength from 40% ABV upward, filtered or not.

Add water or ice to a non-chill filtered whisky and you lower both the strength and the temperature. The long-chain esters drop out of solution and the whisky clouds.

It is a sign that those compounds are present. It says nothing about quality on its own. Many cask strength whiskies, which are usually not chill filtered, cloud strongly when diluted. Our guide to reducing whisky to bottling strength explains how distillers manage haze at bottling.

This is the argument. Supporters of non-chill filtration say it keeps texture and some aroma that filtering strips out. Others say that, at the temperatures and filter grades most producers use, the difference is small and hard to detect blind. Published opinion goes both ways.

The fair answer is to taste for yourself. Pick two whiskies from the same distillery, one chill filtered and one not, at similar strength if you can. Taste them blind, side by side, with a little water.

Blind matters. Knowing which glass is non-chill filtered makes most people find more body in it. A friend pouring the glasses out of sight removes that bias.

In much of India, room temperature is warm for most of the year, so a non-chill filtered bottle on a shelf rarely gets cold enough to haze. The haze appears when whisky meets ice or chilled water, which is how many people in India drink it. A whisky that is crystal clear in the bottle can turn cloudy the moment it hits a glass of ice.

Knowing why helps. A hazy glass is not a sign of a fake or a spoiled bottle. Our guide to water hardness and haze explains a separate kind of haze that hard water can cause.

Producers who skip chill filtration usually say so, with phrases such as non-chill filtered or unchill filtered. If the label says nothing, the whisky may or may not have been chill filtered. Strength is a clue. A whisky at 40% ABV that stays perfectly clear over ice has very likely been chill filtered.

Labelling rules differ by country. Indian state rules vary too, so the absence of a claim tells you little on its own.

Take a non-chill filtered whisky and pour two small measures. Add an ice cube to one and a few drops of room temperature water to the other. Watch which one clouds and how fast. Nose and taste both slowly. Keep water on the table, pace yourself and never drink and drive. You will learn more about haze in five minutes than from any label.
faqs: Why does whisky go cloudy with ice?
Cold and dilution make long-chain fatty acid esters fall out of solution. It is harmless and common in non-chill filtered whisky.
The whisky was not chilled and filtered before bottling, so compounds that can cause haze in the cold were left in.
Why are many non-chill filtered whiskies bottled at 46%?
At around 46% ABV and above, the haze-forming esters tend to stay dissolved at room temperature, so the whisky stays clear in the bottle.
